·       Lochia: It is vaginal discharge for 15 days to 21 days maximum. It has peculiar offensive, fishy smell and is alkaline in nature.

·       It is the vaginal discharge for the first fortnight during puerperium

·       The discharge originates from the uterine body, cervix and vagina.

·       It has three types: (Based on the color of the vaginal discharge)

o   Lochia rubra (red color): 3 - 4 days, constituents are blood, decidual and trophoblastic debris.

o   Lochia serosa (brown): 5 days, consists of blood, serum, leukocytes and tissue debris.

o   Lochia Alba (White): 10 - 15 days, contents are leukocytes, deciduas, epithelial cells, mucus, serum and bacteria.

Clinical importance:

·       The discharge may be scanty, especially following premature labor or in case of infection or may be excessive in twin delivery or hydramnios or sub involution of uterus and retained bits of conception.

·       If malodorous, indicates infection. Retained plug or cotton piece inside the vagina can also be a cause, should be kept in mind.

·       Persistence of red color beyond the normal limit signifies subinvolution or retained bits of conceptus.

Here the serum concentration of lactate or lactic acid is persistently 5 mmol/L or greater and there is significant acidemia and serum pH<7.35. So, option (c) is correct.
  • Ringer’s Lactate has a composition similar to extracellular fluid. So, it can be in case of fluid loss as bile or diarrhea. So, it’s not a correct answer.
  • Hypovolemia is usually corrected with Ringer’s lactate because this Ringer’s lactate is isotonic solution. So, option (b) is incorrect.
  • Ringer’s lactate is used for replacing fluids and electrolytes in those who have low blood volume or low blood pressure. It may be used to treat metabolic acidosis. So, this is incorrect response.

• Presence of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) is the serological marker to establish the diagnosis of Hepatitis B. If the serological marker is present after 6 months, it indicates a carrier or chronic hepatitis. Hepatitis B early antigen (HBeAg) is detected in the blood about one week after the appearance of HBsAg and its presence determines the infective state. So, mothers profile likely to be positive for HBsAg and HBeAg. So, option (d) is correct.
  • HBsAg positive indicates hepatitis B. But anti HBsAb positive indicates normal status that is negative for hepatitis. So, both these results are not possible for same individual. So, option (a) is incorrect.
  • Mutant hepatitis causes down regulation of HBeAg production. They do not produce HBeAg, but they are capable of multiplication. This hepatitis is referred to as HBeAg negative hepatitis B. So, it’s not a correct answer.
  • Hepatitis B early antigen (HBeAg) is detected in the blood about one week after the appearance of HBsAg. Here, mother is in carrier state, so both are positive. This is incorrect response.
